question:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in correct order.
We have been
P. able to identify certain patterns in
Q. the microbiome and immune response
R. that are clearly linked to the progression and
S. severity of brain injury
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. PQRS.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct order is: We have been able to identify certain patterns in the microbiome and immune response that are clearly linked to the progression and severity of brain injury.

• P logically follows "We have been" because "able to identify" completes the verb phrase "have been able to".

• Q follows P because "identify certain patterns in" needs an object, which is "the microbiome and immune response".

• R follows Q because the patterns "that are clearly linked to the progression and" describe/qualify "the microbiome and immune response".

• S follows R because "severity of brain injury" completes the phrase "progression and severity of brain injury".

Therefore, the correct order is P-Q-R-S, and the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (PQSR) is incorrect because it places S (severity of brain injury) before R (that are clearly linked to the progression and), breaking the logical link between "progression and" and "severity of brain injury".

• Option 2 (QPSR) is incorrect because it begins with Q (the microbiome and immune response), which cannot directly follow "We have been" without the verb phrase "able to identify" from P.

• Option 3 (RSPQ) is incorrect because it begins with R, which needs an antecedent (the microbiome and immune response) to refer back to with "that", but no such antecedent has yet been introduced.

NOTE

• In parajumble/sentence-rearrangement questions, always locate the segment that logically follows the fixed opening line first, then trace subject-verb-object and pronoun/relative-clause (that/which/who) connections to fix the rest of the order.

• Relative pronouns like "that" and "which" always refer back to a noun that must appear immediately before them in the sequence.

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been underlined and given as options. Select the option that contains an error.
Has Gita any previous knowledge of work with junior colleagues?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. work.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in the word "work". The phrase "knowledge of work with junior colleagues" should be "knowledge of working with junior colleagues".

• Rule — Preposition + Gerund: When a verb follows a preposition (here, "of"), it must take the -ing (gerund) form, not the base/noun form.

◦ Example: She has experience of managing (not manage) large teams.

• Here, "work with junior colleagues" describes the action of collaborating with colleagues, so it must be the gerund "working with", not the noun "work".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "with" is correct as used; it correctly connects "working" to "junior colleagues".

• Option 2: "Has" is correct; in formal/British English, "have" as a main verb can be directly inverted to form a question ("Has Gita any knowledge...?"), without needing "does".

• Option 3: "any" is correct; "any" is the appropriate determiner to use with an uncountable noun like "knowledge" in a question.

NOTE

• Common prepositions that must be followed by a gerund (verb + -ing): of, in, on, at, for, about, by, without.

• Do not confuse this rule with modal/auxiliary + base verb constructions (e.g., "can work", "will work"), where no preposition is involved.

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Neccessary.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Necessary", not "Neccessary". The correct spelling has one "c" and two "s": N-E-C-E-S-S-A-R-Y.

• Spelling key: remember "one Collar, two Sleeves" — one c, two s's — to avoid the common mistake of doubling the wrong letter.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Cemetery" is spelt correctly — a burial ground, spelt with three e's (C-E-M-E-T-E-R-Y).

• Option 2: "Accommodate" is spelt correctly — it has a double c and a double m (A-C-C-O-M-M-O-D-A-T-E).

• Option 3: "Intruder" is spelt correctly — a person who enters a place without permission (I-N-T-R-U-D-E-R).

NOTE

• Other commonly confused spellings frequently tested in SSC exams: Occurrence, Embarrass, Millennium, Harass, Questionnaire, Definitely, Separate.

• Mnemonic for "necessary": it is "necessary" to have one collar (c) and two socks (s).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The monster trucks have very _______ engines, they can probably pull a train coach without any problem.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. powerful.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Powerful" means having great strength, force, or capability — exactly what is needed to describe engines strong enough to pull a train coach. (शक्तिशाली)

◦ Example: The powerful engine of the truck allowed it to tow the heavy trailer with ease.

• The sentence talks about the physical strength/capability of the engines to perform a demanding task (pulling a train coach), which is best expressed by "powerful", the standard collocation used with "engine".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Dominant" (प्रभावी/प्रबल) means having the most influence or control over others; it does not describe the physical strength of an engine.

• Option 2: "Forceful" (जोरदार) means full of force or assertiveness, usually describing a person's manner, argument, or personality rather than the mechanical strength of an engine.

• Option 3: "Impressive" (प्रभावशाली) means causing admiration through size, quality, or skill; it describes an impression created, not the raw mechanical strength needed here.

NOTE

• "Powerful" is the standard collocation with engines, machines, vehicles, and motors when describing their strength or capacity.

• Do not confuse "powerful" (having power/strength) with "forceful" (showing force in behaviour/expression) or "dominant" (having control/authority).

question: Select the sentence that contains no spelling errors.
option_1: Our government has launched a relatively extensive set of reforms for aborgines in the country.
option_2: Our government has launched a relatively extensive set of reforms for aborigines in the country.
option_3: Our government has launched a relatively extensive set of reforms for aboregynes in the country.
option_4: Our government has launched a relatively extensive set of reforms for aborigynes in the country.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Our government has launched a relatively extensive set of reforms for aborigines in the country.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Aborigines" — the original or earliest known inhabitants of a country or region, especially of Australia. Spelled: A-B-O-R-I-G-I-N-E-S.

• Spelling key: AB + ORIGIN + ES — the word is built around the root "origin" (as aborigines are the original inhabitants), which helps in remembering the correct sequence of letters.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "aborgines" is incorrect; the "i" after "or" has been dropped from the correct spelling "aborigines".

• Option 3: "aboregynes" is incorrect; the letters have been jumbled — "e" replaces "i" and "y" replaces "i", distorting the root "origin".

• Option 4: "aborigynes" is incorrect; the "i" before the final syllable has been wrongly replaced with "y".

NOTE

• Remembering that "aborigines" contains the word "origin" helps avoid common misspellings.

• Other commonly misspelt words with similar tricky vowel sequences: Indigenous, Vernacular, Autochthonous.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The contingent managed to ___________ successfully.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. close the deal.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "close the deal" means to successfully complete or finalize a business agreement or negotiation. (सौदा सफलतापूर्वक पूरा करना)

◦ Example: After months of negotiation, the two companies finally managed to close the deal.

• The sentence requires a verb-object collocation meaning "to successfully complete a transaction", and "close" is the standard verb used with "deal" in this sense.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "park the deal" is not a standard English collocation and does not convey the meaning of successful completion.

• Option 3: "heal the deal" is meaningless in this context; "heal" is used for recovering from injury or illness, not for finalizing agreements.

• Option 4: "catch the deal" is not an idiomatic or grammatically appropriate collocation with "deal".

NOTE

• Other common business collocations: "strike a deal" (to reach an agreement), "seal the deal" (to make an agreement final and certain), "broker a deal" (to arrange a deal between two parties).

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the bracketed word to fill in the blank.
For Rahul, everything was a _________ (modern) experience until he stepped onto the field.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. new.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "new" is the most appropriate synonym of "modern" in this context, meaning recently encountered, current, or unfamiliar until now. (नया/आधुनिक)

◦ Example: For someone visiting a big city for the first time, everything feels like a new experience.

• The sentence describes Rahul's experience as "modern" i.e. something unfamiliar and current to him, which is best conveyed by "new" — an experience he had not encountered before.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "flashy" (भड़कीला) means showy or gaudy in an attempt to impress; it does not convey the sense of "modern".

• Option 3: "global" (वैश्विक) means relating to the whole world; it does not carry the sense of "contemporary/current" required here.

• Option 4: "Asiatic" (एशियाई) means relating to Asia; it is unrelated to the meaning of "modern".

NOTE

• Other common synonyms of "modern": contemporary, current, up-to-date, present-day, recent.

• In synonym questions, always choose the word that fits the exact context/nuance, not just any dictionary synonym.

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
Rehan and Ronit are / good friends and / it don't matter to them / as to who is wealthier.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. it don't matter to them.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The segment "it don't matter to them" contains a subject-verb agreement error. The pronoun "it" is third person singular, so it must take the singular auxiliary "doesn't", not "don't".

• Rule — Subject-Verb Agreement: Singular subjects (he, she, it, and singular nouns) take the singular verb form "doesn't" in the present tense; only plural subjects (I, we, you, they) take "don't".

◦ Correct: It doesn't matter to them.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "good friends and" is grammatically correct; it simply continues the compound subject description.

• Option 3: "Rehan and Ronit are" is correct; "Rehan and Ronit" is a plural (compound) subject, correctly taking the plural verb "are".

• Option 4: "as to who is wealthier" is correct; "wealthier" is the correct comparative form used to compare two people (Rehan and Ronit).

NOTE

• Always check the subject immediately governing the verb when identifying agreement errors — here "it" (referring to the situation), not "Rehan and Ronit", governs the verb "matter".

• Common SSC trap: sentences with two subjects of different number in the same sentence (a plural subject earlier, then a singular pronoun like "it" later).

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Moral
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Ethical.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Ethical" means relating to principles of right and wrong conduct, which is the closest synonym of "Moral" — concerned with the principles of good and bad behaviour. (नैतिक)

◦ Example: It is a moral/ethical duty to help those in need.

• Both "moral" and "ethical" describe standards of behaviour based on notions of right and wrong, making "Ethical" the best match.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Honourable" (सम्माननीय) means deserving honour and respect; it describes a quality of a person, not a direct synonym of "moral" in the sense of ethical principles.

• Option 3: "Godliness" (धर्मपरायणता) means the quality of being devoutly religious; it is close but refers specifically to piety, not general moral/ethical conduct.

• Option 4: "Symphony" (सिम्फनी) means a long musical composition, and is completely unrelated in meaning to "moral".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "moral": virtuous, righteous, principled, upright.

• Do not confuse "moral" (adjective, relating to right/wrong) with "morale" (noun, meaning confidence/spirit of a group).

question:
Choose the correct meaning of the given idiom.
A skeleton in the cupboard
option_1: A popular fact which is not hidden
option_2: A popular fact to be kept secret
option_3: An embarrassing fact not to be kept secret
option_4: An embarrassing fact to be kept secret
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. An embarrassing fact to be kept secret.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "A skeleton in the cupboard" means an embarrassing or shameful secret that a person or family wishes to keep hidden from others. (छिपा हुआ शर्मनाक रहस्य)

◦ Example: Every family has a skeleton in the cupboard that they don't want anyone to know about.

• The idiom originates from the macabre image of a literal skeleton hidden away in a cupboard/closet — something shameful kept concealed from public view.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "A popular fact which is not hidden" is incorrect because the idiom refers to a fact that IS hidden, not one that is popular/known.

• Option 2: "A popular fact to be kept secret" is incorrect because the idiom refers to an embarrassing/shameful fact, not merely a "popular" one.

• Option 3: "An embarrassing fact not to be kept secret" is incorrect because it reverses the meaning — the idiom means the fact IS meant to be kept secret, not the opposite.

NOTE

• Other idioms related to secrets often asked in SSC: "Let the cat out of the bag" (to reveal a secret), "Under wraps" (kept secret), "To spill the beans" (to disclose confidential information).

question:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in correct order.
The rattlesnake
P. it has specialized Jacobson's
Q. organs, which gives it a heightened
R. knows when to lie low because
S. sense of smell to detect prey
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. RPQS.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct sentence is: The rattlesnake knows when to lie low because it has specialized Jacobson's organs, which gives it a heightened sense of smell to detect prey.

• R follows "The rattlesnake" because "knows when to lie low because" is the main verb phrase introducing the reason clause.

• P follows R because "it has specialized Jacobson's" gives the reason (introduced by "because") for the rattlesnake's behaviour.

• Q follows P because "organs, which gives it a heightened" continues the noun phrase "Jacobson's organs" and introduces the relative clause "which gives it a heightened...".

• S follows Q because "sense of smell to detect prey" completes the phrase "a heightened sense of smell to detect prey".

Therefore, the correct order is R-P-Q-S, and the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 (SPRQ) is incorrect because it begins with S (sense of smell to detect prey), which cannot logically follow "The rattlesnake" directly.

• Option 3 (QSPR) is incorrect because Q (organs, which gives it a heightened) cannot follow "The rattlesnake" without first mentioning "Jacobson's" from P.

• Option 4 (QPRS) is incorrect because it disrupts the cause-effect structure — R (the reason clause with "because") must come immediately after the subject, not after Q and P.

NOTE

• In parajumbles, locate the segment containing the main verb of the sentence (here, "knows" in R) to identify what directly follows the fixed subject.

• Words like "because", "which", and "that" are strong positional clues — they must immediately follow the noun/clause they explain or introduce.

question:
Choose the most appropriate meaning of the underlined word in the given sentence.
Even though Margaret had already eaten a large meal, she could not resist eating two slices of the delectable pie.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Delicious.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Delectable" means highly enjoyable or delicious, especially in taste. (स्वादिष्ट)

◦ Example: The chef prepared a delectable dessert that everyone loved.

• The context — Margaret could not resist eating two slices of pie despite already being full — supports the meaning "delicious", since only a very tasty pie would tempt her further.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Stale" (बासी) means no longer fresh; this is the opposite of what would tempt someone to eat more.

• Option 3: "Nutritious" (पौष्टिक) means containing substances necessary for health/growth; taste, not nutrition, is what "delectable" emphasizes.

• Option 4: "Rotten" (सड़ा हुआ) means decayed or spoiled; this is also the opposite of "delectable".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "delectable": delicious, scrumptious, appetizing, palatable, luscious.

• Antonym of "delectable": distasteful, unpalatable, unappetizing.

question:
Select the correct indirect form of the given sentence.
She said to me, "The charlatan will be breaking into the safe."
option_1: She told me that the charlatan would be breaking into the safe.
option_2: She said to me that the charlatan will be breaking in the safe.
option_3: She said to me that the charlatan can be breaking into the safe.
option_4: She said to me that the charlatan is breaking into the safe.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. She told me that the charlatan would be breaking into the safe.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The direct sentence is in the Future Continuous Tense ("will be breaking"), and the reporting verb "said to" has an object ("me").

• Rule — Reporting Verb: When "said to" is followed by an object (a person), it changes to "told" in indirect speech; the conjunction "that" is added.

• Rule — Tense Change (Future Continuous): "will be + V-ing" in direct speech changes to "would be + V-ing" in indirect speech, since the reporting verb "said" is in the past tense.

◦ Direct: will be breaking → Indirect: would be breaking

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because it keeps the reporting verb as "said to me" instead of changing it to "told me", and also fails to change "will" to "would".

• Option 3 is incorrect because "can be breaking" wrongly changes the modal to "can", which is not the correct backshift of "will be breaking".

• Option 4 is incorrect because "is breaking" wrongly converts the sentence to the Present Continuous instead of retaining the future continuous sense as "would be breaking".

NOTE

• Reporting verb rule: "said to + person" → "told + person"; plain "said" (no object) remains "said" in indirect speech.

• Common tense backshifts: will → would, can → could, may → might, is/am/are → was/were, has/have → had.

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Fly into a passion
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. To become angry suddenly.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Fly into a passion" means to suddenly become extremely angry. (अचानक क्रोधित हो जाना)

◦ Example: He flew into a passion when he found out his car had been scratched.

• Here, "passion" is used in its older sense of "a strong, uncontrolled emotion" (usually anger), and "fly into" conveys the suddenness of the reaction.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "To be aggressive at times" is incorrect; the idiom denotes a sudden burst of anger, not occasional aggression.

• Option 2: "To become aggressive often" is incorrect; the idiom refers to a single sudden outburst, not a repeated/habitual tendency.

• Option 4: "To be always angry" is incorrect; the idiom does not describe a permanent state of anger, only a sudden temporary outburst.

NOTE

• Other "fly" idioms tested in SSC: "Fly off the handle" (to lose one's temper suddenly), "Let fly" (to attack verbally or physically), "Fly in the face of" (to blatantly go against/contradict).

question:
Select the correct passive form of the given sentence.
Shalu has ordered new copies of the album.
option_1: New copies of the album have being ordered by Shalu.
option_2: New copies of the album has been ordered by Shalu.
option_3: New copies of the album has been order by Shalu.
option_4: New copies of the album have been ordered by Shalu.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. New copies of the album have been ordered by Shalu.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "Shalu has ordered new copies of the album" is in the Present Perfect Tense.

• Rule — Present Perfect Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + has/have + V3 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + has/have + been + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "new copies of the album" becomes the subject; it is plural, so the auxiliary is "have"; the verb "ordered" (already V3) is retained; and "Shalu" becomes the agent with "by".

◦ Passive: New copies of the album have been ordered by Shalu.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "have being ordered" uses the wrong participle form; it should be "have been ordered", not "have being ordered".

• Option 2 is incorrect because "has been ordered" uses the singular auxiliary "has" with the plural subject "new copies", violating subject-verb agreement.

• Option 3 is incorrect for the same subject-verb agreement error ("has") and additionally uses the incorrect form "order" instead of the past participle "ordered".

NOTE

• Always check whether the new subject (old object) in the passive voice is singular or plural — it decides whether the auxiliary is "has been" or "have been".

• The past participle (V3) must always be used in passive voice constructions, never the base form (V1).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the given sentence.
God has clearly blessed human beings for his glory.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Cursed.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Blessed" means endowed with divine favour or granted a special benefit/good fortune, while "Cursed" means afflicted with misfortune or subjected to a spoken curse/evil, making it the direct antonym. (अभिशप्त)

◦ Example: The village believed the old house was cursed rather than blessed.

• "Blessed" and "cursed" form a standard opposite pair in English, one representing divine favour and the other divine disfavour/misfortune.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Appointed" (नियुक्त) means formally assigned to a position; it is unrelated to the sense of "favoured" versus "disfavoured".

• Option 2: "Produced" (उत्पन्न किया) means made or brought into existence; it does not express the opposite of being "blessed".

• Option 3: "Applied" (लागू किया) means put into practical use; it has no meaningful relation to "blessed" as an antonym.

NOTE

• Other common antonym pairs tested in SSC: Blessed × Cursed, Divine × Evil, Fortunate × Unfortunate, Sacred × Profane.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
A person in love with himself
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Narcissist.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "Narcissist" is a person who has an excessive interest in or admiration of themselves; a person in love with himself/herself. (आत्ममुग्ध व्यक्ति)

◦ Example: He is such a narcissist that he can talk about nothing but his own achievements.

• The term derives from the Greek myth of Narcissus, a young man who fell in love with his own reflection.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Lunatic" (पागल) means a mentally deranged/insane person; it does not mean someone who loves himself.

• Option 3: "Stoic" (धैर्यवान) means a person who can endure hardship without showing feelings; it is unrelated to self-love.

• Option 4: "Polyglot" (बहुभाषाविद) means a person who knows and can use several languages; it is unrelated to self-love.

NOTE

• Other commonly tested one-word substitutes: Philanthropist (a person who loves mankind), Misanthrope (a person who hates mankind), Egoist (a person who is excessively self-centred).

question:
Select the correct passive form of the given sentence.
He has downloaded the movie on his phone.
option_1: The movie has been downloaded by him on his phone.
option_2: The movie was downloaded by him on his phone.
option_3: The movie is been downloaded by him on his phone.
option_4: The movie are being downloaded by him on his phone.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. The movie has been downloaded by him on his phone.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "He has downloaded the movie on his phone" is in the Present Perfect Tense.

• Rule — Present Perfect Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + has/have + V3 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + has/have + been + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "the movie" becomes the subject; it is singular, so the auxiliary is "has"; the verb "downloaded" (already V3) is retained; and "he" becomes "him" as the agent with "by".

◦ Passive: The movie has been downloaded by him on his phone.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because "was downloaded" is the passive form of the Simple Past Tense, not the Present Perfect Tense used in the original sentence.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "is been downloaded" is an ungrammatical construction; the correct auxiliary combination is "has been", not "is been".

• Option 4 is incorrect because "are being downloaded" is the Present Continuous passive with a plural auxiliary "are", which is wrong both in tense and in number (the subject "the movie" is singular).

NOTE

• Present Perfect passive always follows the pattern has/have + been + V3.

• Never mix auxiliaries — "is been" and "are being downloaded" (for Present Perfect) are common SSC distractor errors.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
Giving the worrying impression that something bad is going to happen
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Ominous.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Ominous" means giving the impression that something bad or unpleasant is going to happen; threatening. (अशुभ)

◦ Example: Dark, ominous clouds gathered in the sky before the storm.

• The definition given in the question — "giving the worrying impression that something bad is going to happen" — is the exact dictionary meaning of "ominous".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Desolate" (उजाड़) means deserted, empty, and dismal; it describes a bleak place, not a warning sign of coming trouble.

• Option 2: "Suspicious" (संदेहास्पद) means having or showing a cautious distrust of someone/something; it does not specifically mean "foreboding future harm".

• Option 4: "Bleak" (निराशाजनक) means lacking hope or cheer; it describes a discouraging situation but does not carry the specific sense of "a warning sign of impending harm".

NOTE

• Related words: Foreboding (a feeling that something bad will happen), Portentous (giving a sign that something bad is going to happen), Sinister (giving the impression of evil intent).

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
The new shop that opened last week are hardly sufficient stock of the products that it advertised about.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. hardly had.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The subject of the sentence is "The new shop", which is singular, so it cannot take the plural verb "are".

• Rule — Subject-Verb Agreement & Tense Consistency: A singular subject takes a singular verb, and since the relative clause "that opened last week" is in the Simple Past Tense, the main verb of the sentence should also be in the Simple Past Tense for tense consistency.

• Applying the rule: "are" must be replaced with the singular past-tense form "had", giving "hardly had sufficient stock", meaning the shop barely possessed enough stock.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "hardly hadn't" is incorrect because it introduces a double negative sense (hardly + hadn't) that contradicts the intended meaning of "barely had".

• Option 3: "hardly is having" is incorrect because it mixes a present continuous auxiliary ("is having") with a sentence that is clearly set in the past tense ("opened last week").

• Option 4: "is had" is incorrect because "is had" is an ungrammatical passive-like construction with no valid grammatical form in English, and it also omits "hardly", which is essential to the meaning.

NOTE

• "Hardly" is a near-negative adverb meaning "barely/scarcely"; it should not be combined with another negative word like "hadn't" (double negative error).

• Always match the tense of the main verb with the tense established in the rest of the sentence (here, the past tense set by "opened last week").

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The Romans had developed a (1)________ for chariot racing. The (2)________ of the game are so excited that sometimes it may (3)________ into chaos, confusion and riots. The (4)________ in which racing took place was called a circus. The (5)________ one was the Circus Maximus in Rome, that could hold up to 3,85,000 spectators, which shows the popularity of the sport

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. taste.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "developed a taste for" is a standard collocation meaning to acquire a liking or fondness for something.

• In the context of the passage, the Romans grew to enjoy and appreciate chariot racing, which is best expressed as "developed a taste for chariot racing".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "spoonful" refers to the amount a spoon can hold; it does not collocate with "developed... for" in this context.

• Option 3: "drop" refers to a small quantity of liquid; it is meaningless when combined with "developed a drop for".

• Option 4: "mouthful" refers to the amount of food that fills the mouth, or a long/complicated word or phrase; it does not fit the collocation "developed a __ for".

NOTE

• Common collocations with "taste": "acquired taste" (a liking developed over time), "a taste for adventure", "in bad/good taste" (referring to manners or judgement).

solution_text:

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank refers to the people who watch and follow chariot racing — i.e., its "supporters" or fans, who could get so excited that the events sometimes turned into riots.

• The context (excitement leading to "chaos, confusion and riots") fits the behaviour of enthusiastic fans/supporters of a sport, not political or social "campaigners" or "reformers".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "campaigners" refers to people who organize or take part in a campaign (usually political/social); it does not fit the context of sports spectators.

• Option 2: "reformers" refers to people who work to bring about social or political change; it is unrelated to spectators of a sporting event.

• Option 3: "champions" usually refers to winners of a contest or people who advocate strongly for a cause; it does not fit the sense of excited spectators here.

NOTE

• In passages about sports, words like "supporters", "fans", "spectators", "audience" are commonly the correct fit for describing people who watch and get excited about an event.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. convert.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "convert into" is the standard collocation meaning to change or turn into something else, which fits the context of excitement changing into chaos, confusion, and riots.

• The sentence describes a transformation from one state (excitement) into another (chaos), which is best expressed using "convert into".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "adapt" means to adjust to new conditions; it does not collocate with "into" to mean "turn into" in this sense.

• Option 2: "reshape" means to give a new form or shape to something; it is not typically followed by "into" and does not fit the idea of turning into chaos.

• Option 3: "transfigure" means to transform into a more beautiful or elevated form; its connotation (a positive transformation) is the opposite of turning into chaos/riots.

NOTE

• Common collocation: "convert into" (to change into a different form or state). Compare with "turn into", "transform into", which carry similar meanings.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The Romans had developed a (1)________ for chariot racing. The (2)________ of the game are so excited that sometimes it may (3)________ into chaos, confusion and riots. The (4)________ in which racing took place was called a circus. The (5)________ one was the Circus Maximus in Rome, that could hold up to 3,85,000 spectators, which shows the popularity of the sport

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. stadium.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank refers to the type of venue in which chariot racing took place, which the passage itself then defines as being called a circus — a large open-air venue for public events, essentially a type of stadium.

• The following sentence describes the "Circus Maximus" as holding up to 3,85,000 spectators, confirming that the word being defined is a large venue/arena, i.e., a "stadium".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "circuit" usually refers to a roughly circular route or a racing track (e.g., a Formula 1 circuit), not the enclosed venue itself, and does not fit as naturally as "stadium", which is then specifically called a "circus".

• Option 3: "route" refers to a course or way taken to get from one place to another; it does not describe an enclosed venue holding thousands of spectators.

• Option 4: "track" refers to the specific path on which the race is run, not the entire venue/structure that could hold hundreds of thousands of spectators.

NOTE

• Distinguish between "track" (the racing path itself), "circuit" (a racing route), and "stadium" (the entire structure/venue housing the event and spectators) — SSC passages often test this venue-vs-path distinction.

question:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

The Romans had developed a (1)________ for chariot racing. The (2)________ of the game are so excited that sometimes it may (3)________ into chaos, confusion and riots. The (4)________ in which racing took place was called a circus. The (5)________ one was the Circus Maximus in Rome, that could hold up to 3,85,000 spectators, which shows the popularity of the sport

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. largest.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank compares the Circus Maximus with other circuses/venues implied earlier in the passage, and since more than two items are being compared, the superlative degree is required.

• Rule — Degrees of Comparison: When comparing more than two items, the superlative form (largest, highest, best, etc.) is used, not the comparative form (larger, higher, better).

• Since the sentence describes the Circus Maximus as holding the greatest number of spectators (up to 3,85,000) among all such venues, the correct word is the superlative "largest", referring to its size/capacity.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "larger" is the comparative form, used to compare only two items; it is incorrect here since many circuses are being implicitly compared.

• Option 2: "highest" refers to height/altitude, not to the size/capacity of a venue, so it is contextually inappropriate even though it is superlative in form.

• Option 4: "higher" is both the wrong degree (comparative, not superlative) and the wrong quality (height rather than size/capacity).

NOTE

• Superlative degree is used when comparing three or more things; comparative degree is used only for exactly two things.

• "Large/larger/largest" refers to size or capacity, while "high/higher/highest" refers to height or altitude — do not confuse the two when choosing based on context.
